chapter_theme: Thirumurugatruppadai is a guide poem in which one who has received the god's grace directs another seeker to Murugan: after a 66-line opening sentence that ends in the promise that the seeker will have what he wants, it describes the god at six places (Parankunram, Alaivay, Avinankudi, Eragam, every hill, and Pazhamudircholai with all the places of his worship), each with its own worshippers, and closes by scripting the seeker's praise, the god's appearance and his gift, and the waterfall of his hill.
structure_note: Six sections, each closing on a refrain of right (உரியன், அதாஅன்று; நின்றதன் பண்பே). Twelve of the 21 core units were moved to sentence breaks inside the sections, giving 18 units.

pattupattu:1:1-11.reading: The god's far-reaching brightness is first likened to the sun that the world praises, rising out of the sea; then he is named by his works, feet that bore up those who came to him and a great hand that wore down his foes, as the husband of a bright-browed woman of spotless chastity, wearing on his chest a cool rolling garland from the kadamba of a forest freshly soaked by the first rains.
pattupattu:1:1-11.nuance: Lines 4 and 5 are built as a pair (உறுநர்த் தாங்கிய ... நோன்றாள், செறுநர்த் தேய்த்த ... தடக்கை): the same god is shelter to those who come and ruin to those who oppose, which is the whole promise the guide will make. The consort of line 6 is not named.
pattupattu:1:1-11.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 1-16: the opening description of the god closes at மார்பினன் in line 11, and line 12 turns to his hill and its women.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's form and deeds: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து, under paadaan (porul 2.27)

comparisons.tenor: the great hand that wore down his enemies

pattupattu:1:12-37.reading: On the god's high hill, women with anklets on small red feet, cloth as red as the cochineal insect and girdles strung with coins dress their parted hair with vetchi and kuvalai petals, set a tilakam on the brow, tuck in champak and marutham clusters, hang pindi shoots in their ears, smear their young breasts with sandal paste and vengai pollen, and pluck and toss the tender leaves of the vila tree.
pattupattu:1:12-37.nuance: The women are not named until line 41 (சூரர மகளிர், the fearsome maidens of the hill), so this long toilet scene is a description of goddesses of the slope, not of mortal girls; the flowers they wear are of every land, and the poem does not comment on it.
pattupattu:1:12-37.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 1-16, 17-32 and 33-48: lines 12 to 44 are one description of the hill's women and the god's garland. This unit takes the women's adornment to line 37, where they toss the vila shoots, before the song they sing in line 38.

thinai_evidence.note: a description of the god's hill and its women inside the praise; no love situation is stated

comparisons.tenor: the scent of the sandal paste

pattupattu:1:38-66.reading: The women sing 'long live the victorious cock banner' and dance in a grove on a slope so dense even the female monkey does not know it; the god wears on his head a cool garland of kaanthal that bees do not swarm, and with his long bright spear entered the cold old sea and cut down Sur at the root, while a dread demoness with dry hair and rolling eyes, owl and snake hanging from her ears, held up a skull and danced the thunangai of the battlefield; this red-speared god of flawless victory is the one, the guide says, that you will reach at once if your heart desires to go to his red feet.
pattupattu:1:38-66.nuance: The poem's first sentence runs 66 lines before its main verb: the sunrise, the hill, the women and the war on Sur all lead to the promise இன்னே பெறுதி நீ முன்னிய வினையே (66), so the whole description serves as the guide's grounds for that promise. Lines 57 and 58 (இருபே ருருவின் ஒருபே ரியாக்கை / அறுவேறு வகையின்) are hard: whether the great body of two forms is Sur's or the god's, and what the six ways are, I cannot settle from the words alone.
pattupattu:1:38-66.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 33-48 and 49-66: begins with the women's song in line 38 and ends at line 66, where முன்னிய வினையே closes the poem's first sentence.

thinai_evidence.note: the god's victory over Sur, praised; the battle is the god's deed, so the thinai stays paadaan

pattupattu:1:67-77.reading: He also has a right to dwell on the hill west of Koodal, the city of crowded mansion streets whose gate, hung with tall war banners, ball and doll, has worn down its enemies; there bees sleep in the thorny-stemmed lotus of the wide muddy fields, hum on the honeyed neythal at dawn, and when the sun is up swarm humming round the pool flowers that open like eyes on the hill.
pattupattu:1:67-77.nuance: The bees' day, from field lotus to dawn neythal to the hill pool, joins the city's farmland to the god's hill: the shrine is placed by walking the eye from the walled city out to the slope, and the war-scarred gate of Koodal is the first thing the seeker passes.

thinai_evidence.note: the first of the god's dwelling places, praised; the refrain உரியன் names his right to each

comparisons.tenor: the pool flowers opening at sunrise

pattupattu:1:78-102.reading: At Alaivay he rides an elephant fast as the wind and irresistible as Death, its scarred, striped brow carrying an unfading garland and frontlet and bells ringing at its sides; gems of five kinds flash like lightning in his crown, gold earrings shine like stars clasping the moon, and each of his six faces does a work: one spreads rays so the dark world shines, one gladly grants boons to those who praise, one watches over the sacrifices of brahmins who keep the mantra rule, one lights the directions like the moon as it searches out the meanings left over, one crushes enemies in battle with a wrathful heart, and one smiles with Valli, the young kuravar girl with a waist like a creeper.
pattupattu:1:78-102.nuance: The six faces are a list of offices (light, boon, sacrifice, knowledge, war, love) rather than a portrait; only the last face is turned toward one person, Valli, and she is placed among the kuravar of the hill, not among the gods.
pattupattu:1:78-102.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 78-90 and 91-108: the six faces (91 to 102) belong with the faces introduced in line 90, and line 103 (ஆங்குஅம் மூவிருமுகனும்) sums them up and turns to the twelve hands.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's form and deeds: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து, under paadaan (porul 2.27)

comparisons.tenor: the flashing of the crown's gems
the gold earrings shining around the face
the face that lights the directions

pattupattu:1:103-125.reading: As the six faces keep their order, each of the twelve hands does its part: one raised for the sages who travel the sky, one at the waist, one on the thigh, one driving the goad, two whirling shield and spear, one at the chest, one with the garland, one swinging the bangle aloft, one ringing the bell, one pouring rain from the blue sky, one crowning the heavenly women with the wedding garland; and with the sky's instruments, horns, white conches and thunder-voiced drums sounding and the peacock crying on his victory banner, he goes swiftly by the sky road to Alaivay, which the world praises: dwelling there is his settled nature.
pattupattu:1:103-125.nuance: Where the faces were given offices in the world, the hands are given gestures, and two of them (rain, line 116; the wedding garland, line 117) reach out to the sky and its women. The god reaches his sea shrine by the sky road (விசும்பு ஆறாக), not over land.
pattupattu:1:103-125.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 91-108 and 109-125: begins at line 103, which sums up the six faces and turns to the twelve hands, and ends at the Alaivay refrain in line 125.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's form and deeds: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து, under paadaan (porul 2.27)

pattupattu:1:126-147.reading: At Avinankudi the sages go first: clothed in bark, hair white as the valampuri conch, bodies shining, deerskin on chests where the flesh has wasted, bones showing, fasting for many days, minds rid of hostility and hatred, knowing what the learned do not and themselves the limit of the learned, having cast out lust and fierce anger and knowing no distress; after them come musicians in spotless clothes like smoke, their gentle hearts trained to the lute, plucking its sweet strings, with flawless women whose bodies glow like mango shoots and whose skin is spotted like gold on a touchstone.
pattupattu:1:126-147.nuance: The sages are described almost wholly by what they have removed (flesh, food, hostility, lust, anger, distress), and that list is what gives them the right to walk in first, ahead of the gods of the next lines.
pattupattu:1:126-147.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 126-142 and 143-159: the sages (126 to 137) and the musicians with their women (138 to 147) are one procession that closes at விளங்க in line 147; line 148 begins the first of the three great gods.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the ascetic's excellence in his own calling, the தாபதப் பக்கம் of vaakai (porul 2.16)

comparisons.tenor: the spots on the women's skin

pattupattu:1:148-159.reading: Then come three lords, each known by banner, mount and deed: the rich one whose long banner bears the many-striped bird that strikes down the snake with venomous fangs and fire-hot breath; the one with the white bull raised on his banner, Uma beside him, three unwinking eyes, who destroyed the three walled cities; and the one with a thousand eyes, who completed a hundred sacrifices, mounted on the neck of the four-tusked elephant.
pattupattu:1:148-159.nuance: None of the three gods is named; they are identified by emblem and deed, and all three come as visitors to the younger god's shrine.
pattupattu:1:148-159.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 143-159: begins at line 148, where the three great gods begin, after the sages' procession closes at 147; ends at line 159 with the third god (செல்வனும்).

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's form and deeds: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து, under paadaan (porul 2.27)

pattupattu:1:160-176.reading: With those three famed lords, who guard the world from their good cities, at their head, and with the four-faced one born of the lotus in mind, the thirty-three gods of four kinds and the eighteen companies, bright as stars in bloom, swift as rising wind, strong as fire in wind and loud as thunder, whirl through the sky and come together to see him and win what they need; and with his flawless consort he rests some days at Avinankudi.
pattupattu:1:160-176.nuance: Lines 160 to 168 are hard: why the four-faced one is 'pointed to' (நான்முக ஒருவற் சுட்டி) and what high state the gods seek (உயர்நிலை பெறீஇயர்) are not said. One later reading takes it as the gods coming to ask for Brahma's release; the words here say only that they come with a need (உறுகுறை).

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's form and deeds: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து, under paadaan (porul 2.27)

pattupattu:1:177-189.reading: At Eragam, the twice-born of many ancient families, never failing in the six duties, who spent forty-eight years of youth in study, devoted to dharma and rich in the three fires, chant at the proper hours; wearing the fine thread of three strands of nine, their wet cloth drying on them, hands joined above their heads, they praise him, recite with their tongues the rare hidden mantra of six letters, and holding fragrant flowers rejoice; and there he dwells.
pattupattu:1:177-189.nuance: Every number in the passage (six duties, 'the two', forty-eight years, three fires, nine threads, six letters) marks the brahmins' order, and the six-letter mantra (ஆறெழுத்து, line 186) is the only place the idyll names a mantra. இருவர்ச் சுட்டிய (178) is obscure to me: it may mean families traced from both parents.

thinai_evidence.note: the brahmin's six duties praised: the பார்ப்பனப் பக்கம் of vaakai (porul 2.16)

pattupattu:1:190-205.reading: On the hills the velan wears a garland of green naRai pods with wild jasmine and white koothaalam, his chest smeared with fragrant sandal; the hunters with their cruel bows, drinking with their kin in the small hill village the toddy matured in long bamboo, dance the kuravai to the small thondagam drum; and the women, their hair bound with flowers from deep pools, kulai leaves and the white clusters of red-stemmed kadamba, wearing skirts of cool leaves strung for the bees, walk with the soft gait of peacocks.
pattupattu:1:190-205.nuance: This is the only section of the idyll where the worshippers are the people of the land itself, the velan, the hunters and their women, drinking and dancing, rather than sages, gods or brahmins.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill people's festival for the god, inside the praise

pattupattu:1:206-217.reading: The god himself is red, in red clothes, with tender seyalai shoots swaying at his ears, wearing waistband, anklets and a garland of red ixora, with flute, horn and many small instruments, the ram and the peacock, and the flawless cock on his banner; tall, with bangled shoulders, among women whose voices are sweet as plucked strings, wearing a fine cloth that reaches the ground, he takes the many soft-shouldered does in his drum-like arms and leads them: dancing on every hill is his settled nature.
pattupattu:1:206-217.nuance: The god is described in the same list form as the hill people of the previous lines, with the same red garland, instruments and women: on the hills he is one of the dancers, leading the kuravai, not a figure carried through the sky as at Alaivay.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's form and deeds: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து, under paadaan (porul 2.27)

comparisons.tenor: the women he leads in the dance

pattupattu:1:218-226.reading: He is found wherever he is worshipped: at the festivals each town holds, where small millet is mixed with flowers, a kid is cut and the cock banner is set up; wherever devotees praise him; at the veri ground the velan prepares; in forests, groves and lovely river islets, at rivers and tanks and many other places, at crossroads and junctions and under fresh-flowered kadamba, in the common ground, the hall and at the sacred post.
pattupattu:1:218-226.nuance: The list moves from the town's festival to the open country, the crossroads and a single kadamba tree: the god's places are not only the named shrines but any spot where he is called, which is why the guide will say 'whatever the place may be' (ஆண்டாண்டு ஆயினும் ஆக, line 250).
pattupattu:1:218-226.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 218-233: lines 218 to 226 list the places of his worship, ending at கந்துடை நிலையினும்; line 227 begins the rite itself, which runs to line 249.

thinai_evidence.note: the places of the god's worship listed, inside the praise

pattupattu:1:227-249.reading: There the rite is performed: the place is washed with a fine banner raised, smeared with ghee and white mustard, words murmured and bows made, rich flowers scattered, two clothes of contrasting colour worn, a red thread tied, white puffed rice strewn, pure white rice mixed with the blood of a strong fat ram set out in small offerings in many baskets, turmeric and fragrant water sprinkled, cool oleander garlands cut in pairs and hung, the hill town praised, incense raised and the kurinji tune sung; with waterfall and instruments sounding, flowers scattered so that all fear, and red millet spread with blood, the kuramagal sets up Murugu's music in the dread great house where the god is brought, horns are blown and curved bells rung, the unyielding elephant is praised, and those who seek obtain what they sought; so it is known that he dwells in each place.
pattupattu:1:227-249.nuance: முருகாற்றுப் படுத்த (244), 'where Murugu is guided in', uses the same verb as the poem's own title: the priestess guides the god to the worshippers just as the poem guides the worshipper to the god. The rite is presented as effective without qualification (வேண்டுநர் வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தினர், 248).
pattupattu:1:227-249.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 218-233 and 234-249: begins at line 227, where the rite begins after the list of places, and ends at line 249, which closes places and rites with அறிந்த வாறே.

thinai_evidence.note: the worship rite that brings the god, inside the praise

pattupattu:1:250-265.reading: Whatever the place, when you first see him, praise him with a glad face, worship with joined hands, bow to touch his feet, and say: lord of six dwellings, born of the six, whom one of the five took into his palm at the blue pool on the high peak; son of the god of the banyan; son of the mountain's daughter; Death to enemies; child of victorious Kotravai; infant of the jewelled ancient one; leader of the army of the gods; garlanded chest; poet who knows the texts; unmatched in war; warrior of peerless strength; wealth of the brahmins; mountain of the words of the wise; husband of the women; bull among men; great lord with the spear in your hand.
pattupattu:1:250-265.nuance: The guide gives the seeker the very words to say: the poem turns from description to a script of address. The epithets of birth name three mothers in a row (the mountain's daughter, Kotravai, the ancient one), and the six of his birth and the six of his dwelling are set side by side (அறுவர் பயந்த ஆறமர் செல்வ).

comparisons.tenor: the god as destroyer of his enemies
the god's store of the words of the wise

pattupattu:1:266-276.reading: ...of undiminished victory, who killed the mountain; lord of kurinji with its sky-touching peaks; bull among poets of praised good speech; Muruga, of great name and rare lineage; famed one who satisfies those who long; red one of gold ornament who gives to the afflicted; tall Vel who shelters suppliants on your fearsome chest that won great wars; god of great name whom the great praise; mighty one whose strength cut down Sur; warrior great in battle; chief!
pattupattu:1:266-276.nuance: The god is praised in the words a bard uses of a patron: one who satisfies those who long (நசையுநர்க்கு ஆர்த்தும்), gives to the afflicted, and shelters suppliants (பரிசிலர்த் தாங்கும்). The puram patron's praise is carried over whole to a god, and he is also made a poet himself (புலவர் ஏறே).
pattupattu:1:266-276.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 266-275 and 276-291: the string of epithets ends at குரிசில் in line 276, closed by எனப்பல; line 277 turns to the seeker's own words.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god as warrior and as giver to suppliants, paadaan

pattupattu:1:277-295.reading: Praising him tirelessly as far as you know, say: 'Since it is hard for living beings to know you to your measure, I have come thinking of your feet, wise one who has no equal'; and before you finish what you meant, his many small attendants of many forms will appear at the festival ground and say, 'Great one, a poor old-mouthed suppliant has come, longing for your generous fame,' praising many sweet and good things; and he, coming in a sky-high form full of divine power, will take his awesome high place, show the young beauty of his fragrant ancient godhead, say 'Fear not; I knew of your coming,' speak kind words lovingly, and give you the rare gift that makes you stand alone in the dark-sea-girt world.
pattupattu:1:277-295.nuance: The scene follows the bard's arrival at a king's court step by step: the suppliant (இரவலன்) is announced by attendants, praised to the patron, reassured, and given a gift; only the gift is different, since it makes him unique in the world rather than rich. நின்னளந்து அறிதல் மன்னுயிர்க்கு அருமையின் (278) gives the reason for coming to the feet at all: the god cannot be known, only approached.
pattupattu:1:277-295.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 276-291 and 292-307: the god's reply that begins in line 291 (அஞ்சல் ஓம்புமதி) runs to the gift in line 295 (பரிசில் நல்குமதி); the waterfall's sentence begins with பலவுடன் at the end of line 295 and is taken whole into the next unit.

thinai_evidence.note: the guide's promise of the patron's gift, the core of the ஆற்றுப்படை, paadaan

pattupattu:1:296-317.reading: The poem closes on the god's waterfall: swaying like many different cloths, carrying agil, rolling whole sandal trunks, tearing up bamboo with its flowered branches, breaking the cool fragrant honeycombs that hang like the sun's disc from the sky-touching peak, mixing in old jackfruit segments, shedding fragrant naga flowers, chilling langur and monkey, drenching the great she-elephant, sweeping along the pearl-bearing tusk of the great tusker so that gold and gems gleam, felling banana trunks and coconut clusters, bending pepper vines, scattering peacocks and the jungle hen, driving the boar and the bear with fur like palmyra fibre into the rock clefts and making the wild bull bellow, it roars down from afar: he is the lord of the hill of Pazhamudircholai.
pattupattu:1:296-317.nuance: The last sentence (296 to 317) is a single torrent through every native thing of the hill, trees, fruit, beasts and birds, and only its last line names the god as lord of the hill: the poem ends by showing the seeker the god's land in motion rather than the god.
pattupattu:1:296-317.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 292-307 and 308-317: begins at line 296, where the waterfall's sentence starts after பரிசில் நல்குமதி in line 295, and runs to the end of the poem, since lines 296 to 317 are one sentence ending in மலைகிழவோனே.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's form and deeds: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து, under paadaan (porul 2.27)

comparisons.tenor: the round honeycombs on the peak

links.note: Nakkirar gives each of the six faces and the twelve hands a work in the world; Arunagirinathar asks to hold the same faces, arms, feet, vel and peacock in thought every day.
links.teaches: The list of the god's faces and arms began as a description of what he does for the world and became, in the later hymn, a sequence to meditate on, so the same inventory moved from cosmology to devotional practice.

links.note: The sages who have cast out lust and fierce anger walk first into Avinankudi; the Siddhar poet clears lust, anger and the great lie out of his heart so that it can become the Lord's bedchamber.
links.teaches: Driving out lust and anger is in the idyll the qualification of a class of sages to approach the god's shrine, and in the later poem the housework every devotee must do to make the heart itself the shrine.

links.note: The idyll's assembly of gods comes with Brahma 'in mind' and a need it does not name; the Thiruppugazh number-poem tells that Murugan imprisoned Brahma and freed him when the three gods came begging at his feet.
links.teaches: If the Thiruppugazh's story is the one behind lines 160 to 165, the oldest Murugan poem already assumes the episode of Brahma's imprisonment, and the later hymn only states outright what the idyll leaves as an allusion.

links.note: Nakkirar's Eragam is the shrine where brahmins recite the rare six-letter mantra; Arunagirinathar's Eragam is where 'the brahmins of the six letters' (ஆறெழுத்து அந்தணர்) praise his feet.
links.teaches: The six-letter brahmins of Eragam pass from Nakkirar's description into Arunagirinathar's epithet almost word for word, showing that the later poet read the shrine through this idyll's line 186.

links.note: Nakkirar defines the brahmins of Eragam by their outward order (six duties, three fires, sacred thread, wet cloth, chanting at set hours); Tirumular defines the true brahmins by meditating on the mantra and riding the chariot of love so as not to sink in maya.
links.teaches: The same figure of the mantra-reciting brahmin is praised by the idyll for keeping the forms and by Tirumular only for the inner love the forms should lead to, which shows the Saiva yogic tradition re-grounding a figure it inherited.

links.note: In the idyll, dancing on every hill with the hill women is the god's settled nature (குன்றுதொறாடலும் நின்றதன் பண்பே); in the Thiruppugazh, Kunruthoradal is the name of a shrine where the hill tribes worship him with frenzied dance (வெறியாடி).
links.teaches: A phrase that in the Sangam idyll describes the god's habit among the hill people became by Arunagirinathar's time the proper name of a shrine, so the idyll's description is the origin of a later place of pilgrimage.

links.note: The idyll finds the god in every outer place of worship, festival ground, veri ground, grove, river, crossroads and kadamba tree; Sivavakkiyar asks what use any puja is while the Lord being sought is within us. On the reading that the Siddhar rejects outer places and rites altogether, the two are incompatible.
links.teaches: The idyll widens the god's presence outward to every spot where he is called, and the Siddhar narrows it to the one place inside the worshipper, so the pair marks the two ends of the Tamil argument over where the divine is met.

links.note: The idyll's rite offers rice mixed with a ram's blood and spreads millet with blood, and calls it worship that brings each seeker what he sought; Tirumular says that in worship the bright flower is not killing other small lives. Read plainly, one counts a killing as part of right worship and the other counts not killing as the best offering.
links.teaches: Blood offering stands in the oldest Murugan poem as an ordinary part of effective worship, so Tirumular's rule that not killing is the true flower is a reform of an existing Tamil practice, not a restatement of it.

links.note: The idyll says those who worship with offerings of goat's blood and red millet obtain what they ask; Sivavakkiyar says that offering goat and cock at the shrine when you are sick does not stop you wasting away. The claims about whether such offerings work are incompatible.
links.teaches: The Siddhar's mockery of goat and cock sacrifice is aimed at a rite the Sangam idyll describes in detail and promises results from, so his scepticism attacks a claim with a long and respected Tamil history.

links.note: Nakkirar calls the god 'bull among poets of praised good speech' (புலவர் ஏறே); the Thiruppugazh says Murugan delighted in the poems of Keeran (Nakkirar) and taught him grammar.
links.teaches: The idyll's epithet makes the god a poet, and the later tradition turns that into a story in which the idyll's own author becomes the god's pupil, so the poem's praise of the god's speech came back as the poet's legend.

links.note: The seeker says it is hard for living beings to know the god to his measure (நின்னளந்து அறிதல் மன்னுயிர்க்கு அருமையின்); Tirumular says Vishnu, Brahma and the gods, measuring with thought, cannot conceive the Lord, who stands beyond all measuring.
links.teaches: The theme that the god cannot be measured, which Tirumular argues through the gods' failure, is already in the Sangam idyll as the suppliant's reason for coming to the feet, so unknowability led to approach rather than to despair from the start.

links.note: In the idyll the god appears in his own form to a living suppliant and says 'Fear not; I knew of your coming'; in the Thiruppugazh the poet asks that at the moment Death's servants come he appear on the peacock and end his fear.
links.teaches: The god's appearance and his word against fear, which the idyll promises to any suppliant who makes the journey, the later poet saves for the single hour of death, showing how the guide-poem's promise of a meeting became a plea for rescue.

new_concepts.gloss: the guide poem: one who has received a patron's gift directs another seeker to the patron, describing the road and promising the gift

source_issues: Throughout the text the comitative ending -ஒடு after ய and some other letters is printed -அடு (தெய்வ வுத்தியடு 23, ஓடையடு 79, கூகையடு 49, வள்ளியடு 102, மடந்தையடு 175, குளவியடு 191, கொடியடு 219, 227, தொகுதியடு 212, அருவியடு 240, மஞ்சளடு 235): this looks like an encoding loss of the vowel sign ொ, like the TSCII repairs flagged at lines 39, 285 and 291. Karu forms are copied as printed.
Line 173 மருங்கிந்தம் looks like a misprint for மருங்கில் தம்.
Line 188 பெரிந்துஉவந்து looks like a misprint for பெரிது உவந்து.

Line 295 prints நல்கும்;அதி, which reads more naturally as one word with the particle -மதி (நல்குமதி); the semicolon may be an editorial or encoding error. The sentence break used for the units (after பரிசில் நல்கும்) does not depend on it.
Line 314 கருந்கோட்டு has an irregular nasal (expected கருங்கோட்டு).
